corpus.caveat: pod_slug 'pod-1' IS the live canonical slate — the first rung of the compulsory default chain, the walk a learner descends to by not choosing. It was named 'pod-0' until 2026-09-01, when the two sacked pre-metagraph slates that then held the names 'pod-1' (236 rows) and 'pod-0.5' (27 rows) were archived and deleted and this slate was renamed onto its correct name. Documents written before that date say 'pod-0' IS the live pod: that was true then and is not true now.
corpus.variant_key: null on all 231 rows — surface variants and outcome branches are indistinguishable in the source data

renamed.why: Numbering was retired as a CONTENT label — a walk is named by what it masks — but numbers name the COMPULSORY DEFAULT CHAIN: pod-1, pod-2, pod-3 is the ladder a learner descends by not choosing (Tom's ruling, 2026-09-01). This slate was always the first rung; it had never been named as one.

source.surface_text: populated once, read-only, from canonical_pod_scenarios on 2026-08-30. No writes were issued.

format: A walk is a sequence of NODE REFERENCES. Each step names a node and a position; the surface sentence is a property of the step, never the step itself. Coverage is computable without parsing any prose.

accounting.gap: The document states 47 complete walks and enumerates none of them. The 16 walks encoded here are the ones the document names by attestation run in §2, §3, §4 and §6 — a representative subset covering 12 of the 12 pod-1 nodes, 18 of the 19 composition edges and 10 of the 10 corpus survivability edges. The remaining complete walks, carrying the rows counted in rows_on_complete_walks_not_yet_placed, are a NAMED GAP and are not encoded.

walks.name: First conversation — the whole relational layer

steps.speaker: Learner
steps.surface: Would you mind if I tried to practise speaking [target language] with you? I haven't been learning for very long, and I still feel a little nervous about speaking with other people.

steps.speaker: Friend
steps.surface: Of course, no problem. You seem to speak it very well. I can understand you easily.

steps.speaker: Learner
steps.surface: Thank you, that's good to know. I need to learn more words, and I need to practise listening. I don't understand people very well when they don't speak slowly.
steps.note: S8 — self-account

steps.speaker: Friend
steps.surface: Am I speaking slowly enough for you now?

steps.speaker: Learner
steps.surface: Yes, thank you. It's easier talking to just one person. It's a bit difficult thinking of something to say, though. I'm not sure what to say, but I feel as if I can speak enough to start having conversations.

steps.speaker: Friend
steps.surface: I think you're doing very well. I'm impressed. I think you're ready to start speaking [target language] to anyone who speaks [target language].
steps.note: the corpus’s only disagreement of any kind

steps.speaker: Learner
steps.surface: It's just a little frustrating when I can't think quickly enough to express myself properly. But I know that I need to keep practising if I want to speak more confidently.

steps.speaker: Friend
steps.surface: You should be confident already. I think you're doing much better than you realise. I feel comfortable speaking with you, and I'm not talking very slowly.

steps.speaker: Learner
steps.surface: This is exactly the kind of practice I need. I think I can feel it changing my brain while we're talking! I really appreciate your help. But it's surprising how tired I get when I'm talking in a language I don't speak very well.

steps.speaker: Friend
steps.surface: I think that's normal. Learning a new language is difficult. But it's so much fun when you start to have conversations, isn't it?

steps.speaker: Learner
steps.surface: It really is. I'm really happy that I can have this much of a conversation. And I hope we'll be able to have more conversations in the future as I keep on getting better.
